questions.stem: Boyle's law states that for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, the volume is

options.text: directly proportional to the absolute temperature

questions.explanation: Boyle's law says $PV$ is constant, so as pressure increases the volume decreases in the same ratio — an inverse proportionality. Squeezing a gas into half the space doubles its pressure.

distractorRationale.a: Direct proportionality would mean squeezing a gas made it bigger, which contradicts experience
distractorRationale.c: That is Charles's law, which holds pressure rather than temperature constant
distractorRationale.d: Volume clearly does depend on pressure, as any bicycle pump demonstrates

questions.stem: Charles's law describes the relationship between

options.text: pressure and volume at constant temperature
volume and absolute temperature at constant pressure
pressure and absolute temperature at constant volume
mass and volume at constant temperature

questions.explanation: Charles's law holds the pressure constant and states that volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature, so $\frac{V}{T}$ is a constant. Heating a gas at constant pressure makes it expand in proportion to its kelvin temperature.

distractorRationale.a: That is Boyle's law
distractorRationale.c: That is the pressure law, sometimes called Gay-Lussac's law
distractorRationale.d: The gas laws all apply to a fixed mass, so mass is not one of the varying quantities

questions.stem: In gas law calculations, temperatures must be expressed in kelvin because

options.text: the kelvin is a smaller unit than the degree Celsius
direct proportionality requires a scale whose zero is absolute zero
the Celsius scale cannot measure high temperatures
pressure is always measured in kelvin as well

questions.explanation: Saying volume is directly proportional to temperature means doubling the temperature doubles the volume. That is only true if the temperature is measured from a genuine zero. On the Celsius scale, going from 1 °C to 2 °C is not a doubling of anything physical, so the proportionality fails.

distractorRationale.a: One kelvin and one Celsius degree are exactly the same size; only the zero point differs
distractorRationale.c: The Celsius scale can express any temperature; the problem is where its zero sits
distractorRationale.d: Pressure is measured in pascals or atmospheres, never in kelvin

questions.stem: A fixed mass of gas occupies 300 cm³ at a pressure of 2.0 atmospheres. Calculate its volume when the pressure is increased to 5.0 atmospheres at constant temperature. Give your answer in cubic centimetres.
questions.explanation: Temperature is constant, so Boyle's law gives $P_1V_1 = P_2V_2$, hence $V_2 = \frac{2.0 \times 300}{5.0} = 120\ \text{cm}^3$. The pressure rose, so the volume must fall, which it does.

questions.stem: A gas occupies 300 cm³ at 27 °C. Calculate its volume at 127 °C if the pressure remains constant. Give your answer in cubic centimetres.
questions.explanation: Convert first: $T_1 = 27 + 273 = 300\ \text{K}$ and $T_2 = 127 + 273 = 400\ \text{K}$. Charles's law gives $V_2 = \frac{V_1T_2}{T_1} = \frac{300 \times 400}{300} = 400\ \text{cm}^3$. Using the Celsius values directly would give a meaningless 1411 cm³.

questions.stem: A gas in a sealed rigid container exerts a pressure of $1.0 \times 10^{5}\ \text{Pa}$ at 300 K. When heated to 450 K, its pressure becomes
questions.explanation: The container is rigid, so the volume is constant and the pressure law applies: $\frac{P_1}{T_1} = \frac{P_2}{T_2}$. Therefore $P_2 = \frac{1.0 \times 10^5 \times 450}{300} = 1.5 \times 10^5\ \text{Pa}$.

distractorRationale.a: Inverted the temperature ratio, using 300 ÷ 450
distractorRationale.c: Assumed the pressure simply doubled without using the actual temperature ratio
distractorRationale.d: Multiplied by 450 without dividing by 300

questions.stem: A fixed mass of gas has a volume of 300 cm³ at a pressure of $2.0 \times 10^{5}\ \text{Pa}$ and a temperature of 300 K. Calculate its volume when the pressure falls to $1.0 \times 10^{5}\ \text{Pa}$ and the temperature rises to 400 K. Give your answer in cubic centimetres.
questions.explanation: Use the general gas equation $\frac{P_1V_1}{T_1} = \frac{P_2V_2}{T_2}$, so $V_2 = \frac{P_1V_1T_2}{P_2T_1} = \frac{2.0 \times 10^5 \times 300 \times 400}{1.0 \times 10^5 \times 300} = 800\ \text{cm}^3$. Both changes act to expand the gas — lower pressure and higher temperature — so a large increase is expected.

questions.stem: For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, a graph of the product $PV$ against $P$ is

options.text: a straight line through the origin
a straight line with negative gradient

questions.explanation: Boyle's law says the product $PV$ is a constant at constant temperature. A quantity that does not change as $P$ varies plots as a horizontal line, so this graph is the clearest experimental test of the law.

distractorRationale.a: A line through the origin would mean PV grows in proportion to P, contradicting Boyle's law
distractorRationale.c: That is the shape of a P against V graph, not PV against P
distractorRationale.d: A negative gradient would mean PV falls as pressure rises, which the law forbids

questions.stem: An air bubble of volume 2.0 cm³ is released at the bottom of a lake where the total pressure is 3.0 atmospheres. Calculate its volume just as it reaches the surface, where the pressure is 1.0 atmosphere, assuming the temperature is unchanged. Give your answer in cubic centimetres.
questions.explanation: The temperature is constant, so Boyle's law applies: $P_1V_1 = P_2V_2$, giving $V_2 = \frac{3.0 \times 2.0}{1.0} = 6.0\ \text{cm}^3$. The bubble expands to three times its volume as the surrounding pressure falls to a third.

questions.stem: A fixed mass of gas occupying 300 cm³ at 27 °C is cooled at constant pressure to −73 °C. Calculate its new volume. Give your answer in cubic centimetres.
questions.explanation: Convert to kelvin: $T_1 = 27 + 273 = 300\ \text{K}$ and $T_2 = -73 + 273 = 200\ \text{K}$. Charles's law gives $V_2 = \frac{V_1T_2}{T_1} = \frac{300 \times 200}{300} = 200\ \text{cm}^3$. Note that a negative Celsius temperature still gives a positive kelvin value, which is exactly why the conversion matters.

distractorRationale.c: This equation represents the pressure law, which relates pressure and temperature.
distractorRationale.d: This equation represents the general gas equation, which involves all three variables.
